Crest, appearance and size differences

The mobile crest is a distinctive cockatoo feature, often raised with excitement, alertness or uncertainty. White, pink and dark-plumaged species have very different appearances, and a galah is not the same visual or physical proposition as a large Moluccan or sulphur-crested cockatoo. Ask which species a care description concerns rather than treating the group as interchangeable.

Many larger cockatoos are approximately 30–65 cm from bill to tail, though a cockatiel is much smaller and should not be conflated with this broad range. The bill and feet are strong, and the bird needs room for movement as well as safe space around its crest and tail. Adult dimensions are only a starting point for planning sturdy equipment.

Long life and social temperament

Cockatoo lifespan differs widely across species; roughly 25–60 years is a cautious group-level planning range, not an estimate for a particular bird. A home should think beyond the first owner and budget for years of housing, enrichment, food and care. Claims based on exceptional individuals should not be used as an expected age.

Cockatoos are often expressive and strongly interested in company. Individual closeness varies, and a bird that seeks attention still needs calm independent activity. Establish routines with time together, rest and foraging rather than encouraging constant physical dependence.

Calls, communication and learning

Many cockatoos have forceful calls that can be startling indoors and disruptive in close housing. Vocal patterns differ by species and individual, but there is no reliable way to promise a quiet bird. Some may imitate sounds or words; talking is variable and should never be treated as a feature you can purchase.

Cockatoos can learn useful cooperative routines through patient reward-based training, including moving to a stand or entering a carrier. A crest, posture and vocalisation can provide context, but signals need to be understood as part of the whole bird rather than a simple mood label. Training should help with daily care and communication, not demand constant tricks or suppress normal behaviour.

Diet, housing and safe exercise

Offer a balanced, species-appropriate diet based around suitable formulated food and varied fresh produce, with calorie-rich treats measured rather than freely supplied. Cockatoos can be persistent about preferred foods, so changing an established menu calls for patience. Make mealtimes engaging with safe foraging opportunities while ensuring the bird can reach and recognise its food.

Choose sturdy housing with enough room to climb and stretch and plan supervised exercise in a bird-safe area. Chewing and shredding are important activities, so provide safe materials that can be replaced instead of expecting the bird to leave household objects untouched. Feather dust is produced by some cockatoos and may affect home cleaning and environment; consider that practical reality when choosing a room.

Attention, enrichment and household fit

An enrichment plan should alternate shared interaction with food puzzles, safe destruction and quiet independent time. A cockatoo left with little to do may direct energy towards calling or damaging objects. Companionship cannot be reduced to hours spent physically holding a bird: predictable routines and ways to occupy itself are part of social wellbeing.

First-time parrot owners need to assess whether they can manage big emotions, loud calls and daily interaction before being drawn in by an affectionate moment. Families should supervise every child-bird interaction and ensure adults remain responsible for care. The bird needs an undisturbed refuge and should not be passed around as a novelty for visitors.

Behavioural challenges and commitment

Screaming, chewing, close-contact demands or resistance to separation can become difficult if a cockatoo has few alternatives for attention and activity. Responses should focus on routine, enrichment and a fair understanding of the bird's signals, not punishment. Persistent or escalating problems call for suitable experienced guidance and an honest review of whether the household can meet its needs.

A realistic commitment includes noisy days, regular cleaning, a substantial supply of safe chewable materials and cover for holidays or illness. Make a long-term care plan and discuss the role with everyone in the household before buying. The group can be deeply engaging, but affection does not cancel the work of creating boundaries and encouraging independence.
